items.title: Can the Fed Tackle Stubborn Inflation?
items.summary:
To help you understand what is going on in the economy our highly experienced Kiplinger Letter team will keep you abreast of the latest developments and forecasts ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Letter or subscribe ). You'll get all the latest news first by subscribing, but we will publish many (but not all) of the forecasts a few days afterward online. Here’s the latest… 

Inflation is too high. You know it. We know it. The question: When will it get under control? And what will it take to achieve that? After five years of inflation exceeding the Federal Reserve’s goal of 2%, what must the Fed do to rein it in, and at what cost? 

Inflation, now near 4%, can get down to 3%, we think. The gradually higher interest rates the Fed is preparing to implement should help a bit. So will the calendar, as the year-over-year comparison the government uses to calculate inflation each month stops being worsened by this year’s energy price spike. Fuel prices will still be high next spring, but not higher than they were 12 months earlier. That effect alone will yield some good monthly inflation reports. 2027 may even sport a benign headline inflation rate. 

But... Inflation outside of energy is too entrenched after years of running high. This began amid COVID-19 and continued afterward, when wage gains shot up. Now, you see the resulting price rises in many services: Medical care, car repairs, water service, trash pickup, yard work, entertainment, etc. a relentless incline. 

Goods prices aren’t helping. Normally, goods tend to decline a bit in price over time as manufacturers find…
items.t: Can the Fed Tackle Stubborn Inflation?

items.title: Social Security Is Ditching 'Full Retirement Age'
items.summary:
Social Security's benefit formulas aren't changing, but the words the government uses to describe them are. Under the bipartisan Claiming Age Clarity Act , signed into law on November 20, 2026, the Social Security Administration (SSA) will scrap confusing legacy terms like " full retirement age " and " delayed retirement credits " in favor of plain-English labels that spell out exactly what your filing age does to your monthly check.

"Deciding when to claim Social Security is one of the biggest financial choices a senior will ever make. That choice should not hinge on government jargon that hides how much money is at stake. Thanks to the Claiming Age Clarity Act, Americans will now see plainly what they gain by waiting and what they give up by claiming their Social Security benefits early," said Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (MO-08) in a press release . 

Changing a few words on a federal form won't solve Social Security's long-term funding challenges or magically expand anyone's nest egg. What it can do is strip away bureaucratic euphemisms at the exact moment workers are deciding when to file — ensuring that anyone who claims at 62 knows they are choosing the minimum monthly check, and anyone who holds out until 70 knows they are capturing the maximum.

Using "plain language" The Claiming Age Clarity Act ( H.R. 5284 ), sponsored by Reps. Lloyd Smucker (R-PA) and Don Beyer (D-VA) , updates the official terminology the SSA uses to describe retirement claiming ages, without changing benefit formulas, eligibility rules or payout amounts.

items.t: Social Security Is Ditching 'Full Retirement Age'

items.title: Is Anthropic's IPO the Peak of the AI Boom?
items.summary:
On November 19, Anthropic made history with the largest initial public offering ever , raising about $81 billion. Priced at $83 a share, it opened at $111.50, a 34% jump. 

By the time the U.S. markets closed on November 20, ANT shares had retreated to about $89, giving back much of the post-IPO gains. Now, it's trading at about $87.

Was this "peak AI"? Impossible to tell. And a few trading days cannot provide adequate data. The more important question is whether investors are confusing a revolutionary technology with an investment that can succeed at any price.

History offers two lessons.

The dot-com lesson: Being right about technology is not enough In March 2000, the Nasdaq Composite peaked amid extraordinary optimism about the internet. By October 2002, it had fallen nearly 78% .

The internet did not fail. It transformed commerce and communication. But many investors assumed that every company connected to it would prosper, regardless of profits or valuation.

items.title: High-Yield Bond ETFs Pay More Income, But Taxes and Risk Can Take a Bite
items.summary:
As an asset class, bonds generally carry less risk than stocks. The trade-off is they offer lower potential returns. The reasoning comes down to the fundamental difference between equity and debt.

Stocks represent ownership in a company. As a shareholder, you participate in its potential growth through share price appreciation and, where applicable, dividends. But equity holders are also first in line to absorb losses. If a company goes bankrupt and its assets are liquidated, bondholders have a higher claim on whatever value remains, while shareholders receive anything left over.

Bondholders, meanwhile, are lenders. Even if the issuing company performs exceptionally well, their contractual upside is generally limited to receiving scheduled interest payments, known as coupons, and the return of principal at maturity. A more predictable payment structure plus higher priority in bankruptcy help explain why bonds typically offer lower expected returns than equities.

However, certain segments of the bond universe can offer yields that rival those of stocks. One prominent example is high-yield bonds, also known as non-investment-grade bonds or junk bonds . These are rated below BBB- by S&P Global Ratings and Fitch, or below Baa3 by Moody's. 

Such ratings indicate greater credit risk, including a higher likelihood that the issuer could experience financial distress or default. To compensate investors for taking on that additional uncertainty, these bonds typically offer higher yields than investment-grade debt.

Some companies issue bonds with non-investment-grade ratings…
items.t: High-Yield Bond ETFs Pay More Income, But Taxes and Risk Can Take a Bite

items.title: Got an IRMAA Predetermination Notice? You Have 10 Days to Act
items.summary:
When you enroll in Medicare for the first time , you expect to see standard monthly premiums for Part B and Part D. Instead, if IRS tax records show that your income from two years ago exceeded federal thresholds, you will first receive an IRMAA Predetermination Notice from the Social Security Administration (SSA) — a warning sent before your higher surcharge is formally locked in.

Unlike existing beneficiaries who receive IRMAA Determination Notices in the fall, new Medicare enrollees whose IRS records contain incomplete data, pending tax changes or filing status ambiguities get this advance notice first when they first apply for benefits . Fortunately, there is a 10-day window to verify or clarify the tax data Social Security plans to use before your initial premium is finalized. 

Here is why Social Security sends this notice, what is inside and how the timeline works.

4 common triggers of predetermination notices 

(Image credit: Getty Images) When existing Medicare beneficiaries are liable for the income-related monthly adjustment amount ( IRMAA ) during Social Security’s annual fall recalculation — and their IRS tax data is complete — they receive an official Initial Determination Notice . 

But new Medicare enrollees whose IRS records contain missing or irregular information go through a two-step process instead. A predetermination notice is only triggered when SSA’s system detects specific conditions or red flags during the IRS data match that require clarification.

items.title: How Cultural Blind Spots Impact Attorney-Client Trust
items.summary:
Law schools do a good job of preparing students to pass their state's bar exam , but in general, they fail at preparing them to actually practice law. 

At most law schools , faculty have limited experience practicing law and dealing with clients, especially clients from all over the world. This affects their view of the attorney-client relationship.

In our multicultural country, lawyers newly admitted to the bar often discover a different world than they assumed, as "Catherine" from Cleveland described when she reached out to me.

"I recently opened my own law practice after working for a small estate planning law firm for about a year," she wrote in an email. "I am having problems with one of my clients.

"He is a physician, not originally from the United States, and even though we have a signed retainer agreement, he mailed a check for half the amount along with a note that said, 'I am paying for what I feel is warranted.' 

"I discovered that his prior lawyer had a similar experience with him and got out of the case that I am now handling. We are in the middle of a complicated litigation where he has been sued for non-payment of a lease he cosigned.

"I ignored a red flag that was apparent during our first meeting. When I told him that I could see no viable defense and that if the case went to trial, he would most likely lose and be required to pay the other side's attorney's fees and court costs, he nodded in apparent agreement, but then waved his hand and said, 'Don't worry. They will negotiate half of what they are suing for.' 

"Well, Mr. Beaver, they haven't, and…
items.t: How Cultural Blind Spots Impact Attorney-Client Trust

items.title: Should You Skip Black Friday?
items.summary:
If you've been watching the early Black Friday deals roll out and are feeling less than impressed by them, you're not crazy. A slate of studies have emerged that all have similar findings: As much as 33% of the deals offered on Black Friday last year were "fake" deals. 

That is, the deal price was either the same or even higher than the price the product was selling for throughout most of the year. The teams behind these studies expect to see similar misleading deals plaguing this year's Black Friday . 

So, with so many fake Black Friday deals lurking in all these sales, should you skip shopping altogether? Not necessarily. Even with so many misleading discounts, the majority of deals were still legitimate and this can be a great opportunity to cross a lot of names off of your gift list for the holiday season. You just need to plan your deal-hunting accordingly and learn how to spot the difference between real and fake deals. 

A third of Black Friday deals aren't really saving you money Visualping , a website tracking tool that monitors price drops and other page changes, tracked 1,500 products across multiple categories during Black Friday last year. The company will be doing the same this year. Of those 1,500 products, 33% were cheaper before Black Friday than they were during the sales event. 

And it wasn't just a little more expensive either. On average, according to Visualping, these "fake" Black Friday deals were 37% more expensive than the product's lowest observed price. 

Wallethub conducted a similar study comparing Black Friday deal prices on Amazon with the…
items.t: Should You Skip Black Friday?

items.title: I-Bonds vs High-Yield Savings Accounts and CDs: Which is Better For You Now?
items.summary:
If you're looking for a safe place to grow your savings, a 5.5% interest rate on a savings bond may be worth considering. Series I savings bonds, also known as I-bonds , offer a way to earn interest while helping protect your savings against inflation. But how do they compare with more traditional savings options, such as certificates of deposit (CDs) and high-yield savings accounts?

Competitive one-year CDs are currently offering around 4.5% to 4.65% APY, while several high-yield savings accounts are paying around 4% or more. That means savers have several attractive options, each with different benefits and restrictions.

Before moving your money, here's how I-Bonds compare with CDs and high-yield savings accounts , and which option might make the most sense for your financial goals.

How does the new 5.5% I-Bond rate work? An I-Bond earns interest through two components: a fixed rate and an inflation-adjusted rate. The fixed rate is established when you purchase the bond and remains the same for the life of the bond, which could be up to 30 years.

The inflation-adjusted portion of earnings changes every six months and is based on the Consumer Price Index. Together, these two parts determine the bond's composite interest rate. The current I-bond rate of 5.5% was set on November 1, and it applies until April 30, 2027, at which point a new rate will be announced.

However, there's an important catch. The advertised 5.5% rate only applies to the first six months after purchasing an eligible I-bonds. After that, the inflation-adjusted portion resets, which means your total…
items.t: I-Bonds vs High-Yield Savings Accounts and CDs: Which is Better For You Now?

items.summary:
Dear Wealth Wise : I'm 52, and my husband is 54. We make about $200K a year, but we have two kids in college and one is only a freshman. We still have a mortgage, live in a high-tax area, and can't move because my 80-something parents are 15 minutes away and need us. We have about $750K saved for retirement, no pensions. 

My parents live on Social Security plus my dad's small pension. I'm an only child and help support them. I buy groceries and don't ask for money, and my parents don't even realize we're paying some of their bills. The last time a plumber came, it cost $480. We paid him and told my parents it was $125. 

I'm not counting on an inheritance , especially if they need a nursing home, which they might eventually. Their paid-off house is probably worth $500K, and their savings are minimal. 

My husband and I probably provide more than $10K a year in support, which we could use for our own savings and to help pay for college. We don't want our parents to stress. But we're stressed. — Sandwiched Gen X 

Dear Sandwiched Gen X : When you're an only child, it's not unusual for the burden of caring for a parent to fall on you. It's also common to spend money in the course of caring for older parents.

AARP reports that family caregivers spend $11,508 a year on average. And while you and your spouse may be covering general living costs more than medical bills, it's clear you're spending money on your parents that you can't easily spare. That's true even though your $750K in retirement savings is well ahead of typical Gen X balances — for context, the average Gen X…
items.t: We're Gen Xers Secretly Paying My Parents’ Bills

items.title: Knight Kiplinger's Reflections On Our 80-Year Legacy
items.summary:
Kiplinger Personal Finance Magazine is celebrating its 80th birthday. In honor of that, we're sharing articles from the 80th-anniversary print edition, including this reflection from Knight Kiplinger. 

If you are reading these words in a certain format — printed in ink on paper, in a magazine you're holding in your hands — you are witnessing (and supporting) a minor miracle: The survival and prospering of Kiplinger Personal Finance for 80 years. Thank you! (If you're reading these words online, at Kiplinger.com, we love you, too; after all, it's the content that counts.)

Even before the internet began siphoning off subscribers and ad revenue in the early 2000s, magazines had a high mortality rate, coming and going with changing tastes.

Print periodicals that have been continuously published for eight decades are pretty rare. Several of them are in the business and finance field — witness The Economist (founded in 1843) and Dow Jones's Wall Street Journal (1889) and Barron's (1921), and our sister services, The Kiplinger Letter (1923) and The Kiplinger Tax Letter (1925). Their longevity, like this magazine's, seems to suggest that readers will keep seeking out and paying for high-quality, practical information rather than just entertainment or general edification.

items.title: Copper's Bull Case: 3 Less Obvious Stocks to Invest In
items.summary:
Copper is no longer an undiscovered investment theme.

The metal sits at the center of several enormous spending trends, including electric-grid expansion, electric vehicles, renewable power and industrial electrification. AI data centers add another source of demand, but they're only part of the story. 

Worldwide copper demand could rise about 50%, from roughly 28 million metric tons in 2025 to 42 million by 2040, according to recent S&P Global estimates.

The supply side may be even more important.

Copper mines are enormously capital intensive, and major projects can take 10 to 20 years to progress from discovery and development to production. Many of the world's largest mines have already been operating for decades, and aging mines can face declining ore grades, rising costs and increasing technical complexity.

Recent disruptions demonstrate just how difficult existing production can be to replace. A September 2025 mudflow at Freeport-McMoRan's Grasberg operation in Indonesia forced a broad suspension of mining operations at one of the world's largest copper deposits. Freeport expects the recovery process to continue into 2027.

items.summary:
Kiplinger Personal Finance Magazine is celebrating its 80th birthday. In honor of that, we're sharing articles from the 80th-anniversary print edition, including this collection of advice from our 80-year-old peers. 

Eight decades of living yields a lot of wisdom. We asked financial experts and cultural icons who are in their eighties or will turn 80 in 2027 to share their insights and advice about money for their peers and younger generations. 

Here's what they had to say.

Advice for younger people Save, save, and save some more. 

"Save! More! Money! You're lucky if your employer offers retirement investment accounts. If you're on your own, set one up at a low-cost mutual fund. Have, say, 10% swept out of every paycheck and then forget that money is there. Don't raid the funds if you need money, at least not until you have only two carrots left for dinner and the lights are out. If you're young and broke, you can recover, but not if you're old and broke."

— Jane Bryant Quinn , 87, financial journalist, syndicated columnist and best-selling author of How to Make Your Money Last 

Invest in the stock market, early and often.

items.title: 5 Key Risks in the 10-Year Retirement Gap
items.summary:
If you're like most people nearing or in retirement , you've spent 20- to 30-plus years building your retirement savings. You've made sacrifices, saved diligently, invested consistently and watched your portfolio grow. 

But how many of us think about preparing for the next chapter? There's a transition on the horizon that doesn't happen automatically when you punch out for the last time and enter retirement. 

That transition should begin years before your final workday. The decisions you make in the five to 10 years before you retire, and in the first five years after, could shape your financial future more than any other period of your life.

I call this stretch of time the retirement danger gap, and it deserves far more attention than most people give it. It's the bridge between two very different phases: Growing your wealth and living on it while making sure it lasts. 

The ripple effect The gap shows up in the decisions you make during these years and in how those decisions ripple through the rest of your retirement . Making them without a trusted professional by your side can be the difference between a retirement that thrives and one that struggles.

When you were still working, you had two advantages: Time and paychecks. If the market had a rough spot when you were 40 years old, you could shrug it off, knowing you had plenty of time to recover any losses.

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
